options.label: Raise a cup to {heroName} in front of everyone

success.text: The toast lands, the room cheers, and {heroName} buys the next round.

failure.text: Your toast gets the hero's name wrong. The bard puts that in the song too.

options.label: Let the song find its own way

success.text: Songs travel on their own, slowly.

failure.text: The song dies in the taverns within the week. {heroName} hoped for more.

ignored.text: The bard moves on and the song goes with them.

stages.text: {menace} has put gold on {hero}'s head: a name that famous is worth more to the enemy dead. Strangers have been asking at the gates which inn the hero sleeps at.

options.label: Set a trap with {heroName} as the bait

success.text: The killers come at midnight and walk straight into the watch. One of them talks before dawn.

partial.text: The trap springs, but not before a knife finds {heroName}'s ribs.

failure.text: The killers smell the trap and strike a night early. {heroName} lives, barely.

options.label: Put the watch on their door

success.text: Two watchmen sleep across {heroName}'s threshold until the strangers give up and ride on.

options.label: Tell them to watch their back

success.text: You tell {heroName} straight, and they take it well enough: they would rather know.

failure.text: {heroName} hears you out and sleeps with a blade under the pillow. They expected more from the town.

ignored.text: Someone tries for {heroName} in an alley behind the tannery. They live, and they won't forget who did nothing.

stages.text: A rival company off the river barges has heard of {hero} and wants to see if the songs are true. Their captain slaps a gauntlet down on a table at {tavern} and calls {heroName} out.

success.text: The square fills, the stalls do a roaring trade, and {heroName} sends the rival into the horse trough to wild cheering.
You read the rival's nerves right. {heroName} wins in three passes and the town wins the purse.

failure.text: The rival was better than they looked. {heroName} loses, and so does the treasury.

success.text: The order goes up and sticks. {heroName} grumbles about honour, but keeps the peace.

failure.text: The order goes up, and both of them laugh at it. The town sees who was laughed at.

ignored.text: They settle it in the street outside {tavern}. {heroName} wins, but a market stall doesn't.

stages.text: {hero} has been drinking at {tavern} since noon, and the landlord has come to the hall to complain: broken stools, a frightened serving girl, an unpaid slate. People are starting to ask why the town keeps heroes like that.

success.text: The watch walks {heroName} home and the magistrate takes the slate out of their purse.

failure.text: The watch tries, and {heroName} laughs them out of the tavern. It is the watch that looks foolish.

success.text: Away from the crowd {heroName} is ashamed of it. They pay the landlord and apologise to the girl.

failure.text: {heroName} laughs in your face and orders another jug.

success.text: The slate is cleared. The talk isn't.

ignored.text: It ends with a window through the street and the landlord barring the door.

stages.text: A magistrate's rider from downriver comes to the hall with a warrant for {hero}, for a robbery on the river road the year before last. Hand them over, the rider says, or the barges stop calling at {town}.

success.text: {heroName} goes south in irons. The river towns call {town} a lawful place, and the other heroes go quiet.

failure.text: {heroName} goes in chains, but not quietly, and their friends in the hall remember who handed them over.

success.text: You swear {heroName} was here that season, and the rider rides home with a sworn statement instead of a prisoner.

partial.text: The rider takes your word, and a 'fee' for taking it.

failure.text: The rider doesn't believe a word of it. For a month the barges pass {town} by.

success.text: The merchant is made whole, the warrant is torn up, and {heroName} owes the town.

ignored.text: The rider leaves cursing {town} for a den of outlaws, and the river towns believe them.

stages.text: The best smith in {settlement} has walked to {town} with a choice for you. The great forge at home is failing. They could bring their hammers here and work for {town}, or, with {town}'s coin, reline the old forge and make {settlement} a stronger friend.

success.text: The smith moves into {town} with two apprentices and a cart of tools. {leader} of {settlement} sends a cool note about it.

failure.text: The smith stays home, and {people} hear that {town} tried to poach their best hands.

success.text: The smith goes home with {town}'s gold, and within a month the forges of {settlement} roar again.

options.label: Ask them to train apprentices here first

success.text: The smith agrees to a season in {town}, teaching, then goes home to a forge {settlement} rebuilds on the strength of it.

failure.text: The smith hears a town trying to have it both ways, and goes home with nothing settled.

ignored.text: The smith waits three days for an answer, then goes home.

stages.text: {contact} of {settlement}, who remembers {memory}, writes to ask a favour: a loan to see them through a lean season, and a word from {town} to the merchants who will not deal with them.

options.label: Send the loan and the word

success.text: {contact} writes back within the week. {settlement} hears that {town} stands by its friends.

options.label: Put in a word, but no coin

success.text: Your letter to the merchants does the trick on its own. {contact} is grateful.

failure.text: The merchants ignore you, and {contact} is left where they were.

success.text: You read {contact} right: they were ready to leave. They come to {town} with their family.

failure.text: {contact} is stung: they asked for help at home, not a way out of it.

ignored.text: No answer goes to {contact}. They do not write again.

stages.text: {band}, the band {settlement} raised to look after its own, send their captain to {town}. They have more courage than steel, and ask for arms.

success.text: {band} ride home in new mail. {settlement} feels safer for it.

options.label: Let them train with the town's heroes

success.text: A fortnight in {town}'s yard, and {band} go home sharper than they came.

failure.text: The training goes badly: a broken arm and hurt pride.

success.text: You send them off with bread and good advice, and they part as friends, if poorer ones.

failure.text: {band} go home with nothing but the road under their boots.

ignored.text: {band}'s captain waits at the gate a day and goes home.

stages.text: A child chased a dog through a grate and has not come back up. Their mother stands at the opening to {site}, calling down into the dark, and half the street has gathered with lanterns.

options.label: Send the watch down after them

success.text: The watch comes up filthy and grinning, the child on a sergeant's shoulders. They saw what lives down there, and drove it back.

failure.text: The watch finds the child, but one of them is bitten badly and things follow the lanterns back toward the grate.

options.label: Offer a reward to anyone who goes

success.text: A rat-catcher goes down for the purse and brings the child up blinking. The street cheers the mayor's coin.
You lead the prayers at the grate yourself. It is a hard night, but the town comes through it together.

failure.text: The grate is chained. Nobody speaks to the mayor in that street for a long while.

ignored.text: No one comes. The street goes down with its own lanterns, and not all of them come back up.

stages.text: Diggers mending a drain under {town} have broken through into {site} and found a door sealed with old wax and older marks. Something on the far side knocks back when they knock.

options.label: Have a scholar read the marks

success.text: The marks are a binding, still holding. A little fresh wax and the right words, and the knocking stops.

failure.text: The scholar reads the marks aloud, and gets one word wrong. The knocking becomes scratching.

options.label: Brick it up and say nothing

success.text: A wall of new brick goes up in front of the old door. The diggers are paid to forget it.

options.label: Break it open for what lies beyond

success.text: Behind the door, an old treasury and an older skeleton. The coin goes to the town.

failure.text: The door gives, and whatever was behind it is gone into the dark before anyone sees it.

ignored.text: The diggers refuse to go back down. The knocking can be heard in the cellars above.

stories.title: The night-soil men won't go down

stages.text: The night-soil men of {town} have downed their shovels. They say things in {site} have been watching them work, and they will not go back without better pay or a guard.

success.text: Coin steadies their nerves. The drains run, and they keep an eye on the dark for the town.
The mayor walks the first stretch with them, lantern high. Shamed and cheered, they follow.

failure.text: They won't hear it. The town reeks for a week before they are paid off.

success.text: The drains back up and the streets smell. Down below, something likes the quiet.

ignored.text: The drains back up, and the stink drives folk from the low streets.

stages.text: A peddler at {tavern} has a book wrapped in oilcloth that hums when you touch it. They swear it came out of a dead wizard's tower, and want gold for it before anyone asks how.

success.text: The book goes up to the library's shelves. The scholars sit up half the night with it.
The peddler takes a third of the price and a free night's ale. The book is the town's.

failure.text: The peddler takes offence and sells it to a passing tinker instead.

options.label: Have the watch ask where it came from

success.text: It was stolen from a wizard's heirs on the road. They thank the town with the book and a letter of credit.

failure.text: The peddler is gone by morning, book and all.

ignored.text: The peddler moves on, and the book with them.

stages.text: The librarian has a bandaged hand and a story: one of the big books on the top shelf bit them. It has teeth now, and it is eating the books on either side.

options.label: Ask the wizards to bind it

success.text: A mimic, starved and clever. Bound, it coughs up the pages it ate, and one book nobody knew the library had.

failure.text: The binding slips and the thing gets away into the stacks. It takes a week to corner it.

success.text: It squeals in the fire. The library smells of burnt leather for a month.

failure.text: The fire spreads to the shelf. The mimic dies, and so does a good book.

options.label: Hire a company to deal with it

success.text: A pair of heroes take it out in the night, quietly, with a sack.

ignored.text: Nobody comes. The thing on the top shelf eats on.

stages.text: Green smoke pours out of the scholars' rooms: an apprentice tried a working from the books before their master could stop them, and the fire won't go out with water.

success.text: Bucket chains of sand from the river, and it dies. Under the soot, the apprentice's notes show they were close to something.

failure.text: It burns through the night. Half a season's notes are ash.

success.text: White-faced, they say the working backwards, and the fire folds itself up. They will make a fine wizard one day.

failure.text: The working twists. The fire goes out, and the apprentice's eyebrows with it, and the master's best book.

options.label: Pay a priest to bless the water

success.text: Blessed water puts it out, hissing. The scholars grumble at the cost and go back to work.

ignored.text: It burns itself out by morning, along with much of the work.

stages.text: The town clerk brings the mayor the hearth-tax rolls with a frown. Four households paid last spring that nobody in town remembers: not the neighbours, not the priest, not the families on either side. The names are in the clerk's own hand.

options.label: Have the clerks go through every roll

success.text: Three nights by lamplight turn up eleven more. Every one of them lived near the old cellars by the river. The clerk has started sleeping at the town hall.

failure.text: The clerks find nothing more, and by the end of the week the clerk is no longer sure the names were ever there.

options.label: Pay a scholar to look into it

success.text: The scholar comes back pale. The missing households are real, she says, and so is something about how the town forgets them.

options.label: A clerk's error. Let it lie

success.text: The rolls are corrected. Nobody misses the names.

ignored.text: Nobody does anything about the rolls, and nobody remembers why it seemed to matter.

stages.text: A glassmaker in the river ward has covered every mirror in her shop. In them, she says, a girl walks past who is not in the room, and the girl is her own daughter. She has no daughter. {hero} has offered to go down into the cellars the reflection keeps walking toward.

success.text: Under the oldest cellar {hero} finds a stair that is not on any plan, and at the bottom of it, singing. {hero} comes back up with a child's shoe and can no longer stop humming.

partial.text: {hero} finds the hidden stair and hears the singing, and comes back up white and bleeding from the ears.

failure.text: {hero} comes back up an hour later with no memory of going down, and an empty bed in the glassmaker's house is now just an empty bed.

options.label: Have the temple bless every mirror in the ward

success.text: The priests bless the glass and the reflections stop. Under the blessing a faint line of frost leads to an old cellar door.

failure.text: The blessing does nothing. The glassmaker breaks every mirror she owns and leaves town.

options.label: Cover the mirrors and say nothing

success.text: The mirrors are covered. A month from now, two more households will be names nobody remembers.

ignored.text: By the time anyone thinks to act, the glassmaker has forgotten why she covered the mirrors.

stages.text: Below the river ward, in a vault older than the town, something sings. Everyone who hears it long enough is forgotten by everyone who loved them, and walks down to join the choir. {hero} says they can find the singer and stop it.

success.text: {hero} finds the singer, a thing like a wedding veil full of mouths, and cuts it apart in the dark. Up in the town, people start weeping for names they had forgotten, and some of the forgotten walk back up the stair.

partial.text: {hero} kills it, but the vault comes down on the way out, and {hero} is carried home on a door.

failure.text: {hero} does not come back up. The singing gets louder for a week, then softer, as if it had eaten well.

options.label: Wall the vault and bless the stones

success.text: Masons and priests seal the vault under a slab of consecrated stone. The singing stops, or at least nobody can hear it now.

options.label: Leave it an offering, as the old folk did

success.text: A cart of grain and a cask of wine go down the stair every new moon. The singing is quieter, and the town tries not to think about why.

ignored.text: While the council argues, the choir gains another voice.

stages.text: The forgotten households were never forgotten, because they never lived. The deputy clerk invented them, collected their tax, and spent it on a house in the next valley. Half the town had been whispering about a curse.

options.label: Make an example of the clerk

success.text: The clerk is put in the stocks, the money is found under a floorboard, and the town laughs at itself for a week.
The clerk pays back every coin and leaves town before dawn. The curse stories take longer to die.

ignored.text: The clerk is gone before anyone acts, with the money.

stories.title: What drinks at the old cistern

stages.text: The forgotten households all drew their water from the old cistern under the market, the one Caldor's engineers built. A boy who drank there at night says a lady in the water asked him his name, and he can't remember telling her, or what his name was.

success.text: {hero} wades into the dark and finds her: a drowned thing in a court dress, wearing a crown of names. {hero} drags her into the lamplight, and she comes apart like wet paper. The boy remembers his name.

failure.text: {hero} is pulled under and dragged out half-drowned, and the lady in the water now knows {hero}'s name.

success.text: The cistern is filled with rubble and the market loses its old well. Nobody else forgets anyone.

ignored.text: Another household draws water at night.

stages.text: The scouts sent to look at {site} come back uneasy. The "monsters" the farmers want killed are families of goblins, with children, half-starved and fleeing something worse out in the deep country. The farmers who posted the bounty want them gone all the same.

success.text: The goblin families come to the town under a flag of truce. The farmers spit, the children stare, and the newcomers set to work in the tanneries nobody else wants.

options.label: Let them stay where they are, under watch

success.text: You talk the farmers round: the goblins keep to the hollow, trade mushrooms for bread, and the bounty is torn up.

failure.text: The farmers won't hear it. They go out with torches the same night.

success.text: Heroes drive the families out of {site} and into the hills. The farmers cheer. Nobody asks what the goblins were running from.

ignored.text: While the council talks, the farmers settle it themselves, with torches.

stages.text: A goblin child from the families the town took in runs to the gate at dusk: her uncle saw {menace}'s raiders gathering in the hills, and the goblins want the town to know first.

options.label: Thank them, and man the walls

success.text: The raiders find the walls manned and the gates barred, and turn away cursing. In the goblin lanes, they are already telling the story.

options.label: Send them back out to watch the hills

success.text: The goblins watch the hills for the town from now on, and bring word every week.

ignored.text: Nobody listens to a goblin child at the gate. The raiders come anyway.

stages.text: The goblin families driven out of their hollow have found someone to take them in: {menace}. Their scouts know the town's farms, its paths and its weak walls.

options.label: Send an envoy to win them back

success.text: The envoy goes out with bread and an apology. Half the families come back; the rest stay with {menace}, but stop guiding its raids.

failure.text: The envoy comes back with an arrow in his hat.

options.label: Double the watch on the farms

success.text: The watch walks the farm lanes every night. The raids find nothing, and the farmers grumble at the cost.

ignored.text: {menace} knows the town's back ways now.

stages.text: {hero} walks the council chamber with a lit candle and a frown. There is not one ward on these walls, they say: anyone who can whisper a charm can sit outside the window and decide the town's votes. The old powers of the land know it.

success.text: {hero} carves sigils into the lintels and hangs bells that ring for no wind. Any charm laid on a councillor now has to get past {hero} first.

options.label: Pay for wards to be laid once

success.text: {hero} lays the wards for a fee. They will hold for a season or so.

options.label: Councillors can mind their own heads

success.text: The candle gutters. {hero} shrugs and goes back to the tavern.

ignored.text: The chamber stays as it is: walls, benches and nothing else.

stages.text: {hero} asks for a seat by the council door. Their god lets them hear a lie as a sour note, they say, and in a town the dark powers have started to notice, someone ought to be listening.

options.label: Give {hero} the seat by the door

success.text: {hero} sits by the door through every session. Twice in the first month a councillor stops in the middle of a speech and sits down again.

options.label: The council is not on trial

success.text: {hero} bows and leaves. The councillors are relieved, and some of them more relieved than others.

ignored.text: Nobody answers {hero}, and the seat by the door stays empty.

stages.text: Half the children of the lanes follow {hero} about with wooden swords and pot-lid shields, and the other half are the monsters. Their parents are torn between pride and worry: some of the bigger ones talk about going out to find a real lair.

options.label: Have {hero} teach them to hold a stick properly

success.text: {hero} drills them on the green at dawn. The children are proud, the parents are pleased, and the watch has a dozen new recruits waiting to grow up.

options.label: Have {hero} tell them how it really is

success.text: {hero} sits them down and tells them about the friends who didn't come home. The game goes quiet for a few days.
The children play heroes and monsters until dark, and the bravest of them start looking at the hills.

ignored.text: The game goes on, and the bravest of them start looking at the hills.

stages.text: A miller's boy is missing. His friends say he went out before dawn with a kitchen knife and a sack, to find a monster to kill like {hero} does. His mother is at the town hall. {hero} is already pulling on their boots.

success.text: {hero} tracks the boy to a wolf den in the hills and carries him home over one shoulder, both of them muddy and the boy grinning. He is going to be impossible for a year.

partial.text: {hero} finds the boy treed by wolves and gets him down, at the cost of a bad bite.

failure.text: {hero} finds the knife and the sack, and nothing else. The mill is silent for a long time.

options.label: Turn out the watch and the whole lane

success.text: Torches go up and down the hills all night. They find him at dawn, asleep in a hollow tree, cold and furious that nobody let him finish.

ignored.text: By the time anyone goes looking, the trail is cold.

stages.text: Word comes by sending stone: {party} found a girl from the town hidden in their supply wagon, half a day out. She wants to be a hero. She has brought a sword that is mostly rust.

options.label: Send her home with an escort

success.text: One of the company walks her back to the gate, and she gives the watch a full report of the adventure.

options.label: Let her carry the packs and learn

success.text: She carries packs, cooks badly and keeps watch better than anyone. She comes home a squire with a story she will tell until she is old.

failure.text: She wanders off after a glowing light on the second night, and the company spends a day getting her back.

ignored.text: The company makes its own choice, and her mother has words with the mayor.

stages.text: {hero} has dreamed the same dream three nights running: {patron}, {patronTitle}, offers a pact. Power, if {heroName} will give it what it wants. {heroName} asks the mayor what the town would think.

success.text: {heroName} wakes with a mark on their wrist and a new light in their eyes. The town will see what the price is.
{heroName} burns the dream-letter in the tavern hearth. They are not sure they would have said no on their own.
{heroName} talks the patron round in their sleep, and wakes sworn on terms it will regret.

failure.text: The patron does not like being haggled with. {heroName} wakes sworn all the same, and already in its debt.

ignored.text: {heroName} stops talking about the dream. Nobody knows what they answered.

stages.text: {hero} has orders from {patron}. It wants something done in {town} tonight, and it wants the mayor not to ask what.

success.text: Something is done in the night. By morning {heroName} is in better spirits, and nobody can say quite what changed.
The watch sees {heroName} leave a sealed letter under the old bridge, and stop it before it is taken. {patron} is not pleased.

failure.text: The watch loses {heroName} in a fog that rises out of nowhere. The errand is done all the same.

success.text: {heroName} takes the gold and stays at the tavern all night. {patron} remembers.

ignored.text: Whatever {patron} wanted, it got.

stages.text: {hero}'s familiar, {familiar}, got loose in {tavern} last night: the taps are knotted, the barmaid's hair is green and someone's purse is singing.

success.text: {heroName} pays up with a sigh and promises a leash. The familiar sulks for a week.
The story goes round every tavern in {town}, and gets better each time.

options.label: Have a priest bless the tavern

success.text: The blessing sends the familiar squealing home. {patron} takes it as a slight.

failure.text: The holy water turns to ale. The tavern has never been busier.

ignored.text: The familiar goes home on its own when the ale runs out.

stories.title: The Hollow Prince wants a door

stages.text: {hero} brings word from {patron}: it is pleased with {town}, and wants a door. A pit is to be dug under the old well and a stone set at its bottom, and the Prince's court will come and go as it likes. It pays well.

success.text: The stone is set. The well water runs warm now, and the gold comes up in the buckets.
{town} will dig no door for anyone. The Prince's sworn feel the cold of its displeasure.
The priests pour lead into the well and sing over it for a night and a day. Whatever was listening below stops.

failure.text: The lead boils away. Something laughs at the bottom of the well, and {heroName} laughs with it.

ignored.text: Someone digs the pit in the night. Nobody admits to it.

stages.text: {patron} would honour {town} with a revel. {hero} says the hedge at the town's edge will open on midsummer night, and her court will dance in the square until dawn. Those who dance with them are not always the ones who come home.

success.text: The square fills with lanterns no one lit and music no one plays. In the morning {town} is merrier than it has been in years, and two of its people are gone.

options.label: Hold it, but ring the square with iron

success.text: Iron nails in every doorframe. The fey dance, sulk a little, and leave everyone where they found them.

failure.text: The fey take the iron as an insult and the music turns sharp. The revel ends in tears and broken glass.

success.text: Milk and honey left at the hedge, and a polite letter. The Queen is gracious, and does not forget.

ignored.text: The hedge opens anyway. Some dance, some sleep through it.

stories.title: The Ninth Mask asks for the stars

stages.text: {hero} has been drawing star charts on the tavern walls. {patron} wants the town's scholars to watch one patch of sky for a season and write down what they see. It promises secrets in return. It does not say whose.

success.text: The scholars watch, and write, and stop sleeping. The library has never learned so fast.

options.label: Take its secrets, keep our eyes

success.text: The scholars copy down what the Mask shows them without once looking up. It is impressed, and a little annoyed.

failure.text: One of them looks up. She has not stopped talking about it since, and the words are not ours.

success.text: Shutters on every library window. The whispering stops, and so does the Mask's interest in {hero}.

ignored.text: Someone watches anyway. They are found in the morning with their eyes full of stars.

stages.text: {patron} has taken a liking to {town}, and offers the mayor a wager through {hero}: one toss of its coin, the treasury's gold against as much again. It has never been known to cheat. It has never been known to lose, either.

success.text: Heads. The coin spins in the air for a full minute before it lands. The treasury fills overnight, and the Wager laughs like a bell.

failure.text: Tails. The chests in the town hall are lighter by morning. The Wager is gracious in victory.

options.label: Bet only what we can lose

success.text: A small stake, a small win. The Wager calls the mayor a coward, fondly.

failure.text: A small stake, a small loss, and a sneer.

options.label: Refuse to gamble with the town

success.text: The Wager shrugs, and turns its luck on more interesting places.

ignored.text: The Wager takes silence for a refusal.

stages.text: {tavernKeeper} of {tavern} {keeperStory}. Now a pedlar has sold them a sword they swear belonged to one of the four they lost, and they want to know how it came out of the ground.

options.label: Have a hero look into it

success.text: {hero} traces the sword to a barrow-robber and gets the bones back too. {tavernKeeperName} buries their friend at last, and the first round at {tavern} is on the house for a month.

failure.text: The pedlar is gone and the trail is cold. {tavernKeeperName} hangs the sword over the bar and does not talk about it.

options.label: Buy the sword for the wall

success.text: The sword hangs over the bar at {tavern}, and every hero who drinks there toasts the four who never came home.
{tavernKeeperName} nods. They expected nothing else from a town hall.

ignored.text: {tavernKeeperName} stops asking.

stages.text: {tavernKeeper} of {tavern} {keeperStory}. They offer to walk the lanes round {tavern} at closing time with a cudgel, if the town hall will pay for the lamp oil and look the other way when they use it.

success.text: Closing time round {tavern} goes quiet. A few heads are cracked, all of them deserving.
{tavernKeeperName} takes the watch's oath again with tears in their eyes, and drills the young watchmen on their evenings off.

failure.text: The captain of the watch will not have an old sergeant telling his men what to do. Words are said.

success.text: {tavernKeeperName} grumbles that the town has gone soft.

ignored.text: {tavernKeeperName} keeps the peace inside their own walls and leaves the lanes to the dark.

stages.text: {tavernKeeper} of {tavern} {keeperStory}. An old friend has left forty casks of brandy in their cellar that nobody paid duty on, and the friend has not come back for them. They ask the town hall what it would like done.

success.text: The brandy is sold quietly at {tavern} over the winter, and the town hall's share is counted in a back room.
The casks are rolled into the town hall's cellar. {tavernKeeperName} pours a little cheaper for a while, out of spite or relief.
The friend is found sleeping it off in a barn, and pays the duty and a fine to keep it quiet.

failure.text: The friend turns out to have friends, and they come for the brandy one night. Nobody is hurt; everybody is frightened.

ignored.text: One night the casks are simply gone. {tavernKeeperName} says they heard nothing.

stages.text: {tavernKeeper} of {tavern} {keeperStory}. They cannot sing now, but they want to hear {town} sing: a contest at {tavern}, with a silver cup, if the town hall will pay for it.

success.text: Half the town crowds into {tavern} to sing, the other half to boo. {tavernKeeperName} weeps at the winner.
The mayor's choice of winner is cheered to the rafters. The loser's family is not invited next year.

failure.text: The mayor picks the miller's daughter, and the room knows exactly why. It is not forgotten.

success.text: {tavernKeeperName} hums the songs nobody will hear.

ignored.text: {tavern} stays quiet this year.

stages.text: {tavernKeeper} of {tavern} {keeperStory}. They have heard a stranger at their bar asking about the town's walls a little too carefully, and they will say more for a price.

success.text: The stranger is taken at dawn with a sketch of the gates in his boot. {tavernKeeperName} has a new coat by the week's end.
{tavernKeeperName} gives the name for nothing, and never tells the watch anything again.

failure.text: {tavernKeeperName} remembers nothing at all, suddenly. The stranger is gone by morning.

options.label: The town does not buy gossip

success.text: {tavernKeeperName} shrugs. Somebody else will buy it.

ignored.text: {tavernKeeperName} sells the name elsewhere.

stages.text: {tavernKeeper} of {tavern} {keeperStory}. Three children with no family have been sleeping in the stable at {tavern}, and they ask the town hall for help to feed them.

success.text: The children are fed and set to work polishing mugs. The whole of {tavern} adopts them.
A smith, a weaver and a baker each take one. In a few years {town} will have three more trades.

failure.text: Nobody wants them. {tavernKeeperName} keeps them anyway, and lets the town hall know what they think of it.

options.label: The temple can see to them

success.text: The children go to the temple. {tavernKeeperName} visits them every week.

ignored.text: {tavernKeeperName} feeds the children out of their own pocket.

stages.text: {hero} killed {victim} with one blow too many in a tavern brawl. {kin} stand outside the town hall in mourning, and want weregild: blood money for a life, as the old law says.

success.text: The town hall pays, and {kin} take it with stiff faces. {heroName} is grateful, and a little ashamed.
{heroName} counts out the coin in front of {kin} and does not look up. They will not forgive the town for making them do it.

options.label: Try to talk the kin round

success.text: Over a long evening the family is brought to take a smaller sum and {heroName}'s apology, made on their knees.

failure.text: The talk goes badly. {kin} leave the town hall swearing they will have their own justice.

success.text: The mayor rules that a man who throws punches in a tavern takes what comes. {kin} swear a feud on {heroName}.

ignored.text: Nobody at the town hall will see them. {kin} take it to the streets.

stages.text: {hero} scried for the town and took no gold for it. Now they want their favour: the council's seal on a letter that opens a rival's library to them, no questions asked.

success.text: {heroName} takes the sealed letter with a thin smile. Somewhere, a librarian is about to have a bad day.

options.label: Pay them in gold after all

success.text: {heroName} takes the gold, but says a favour was the price, and gold is not a favour.
{heroName} settles for a seat at the next feast and a line in the town's book of honours.

failure.text: {heroName} hears the haggling for what it is, and leaves cold.

success.text: The mayor will not lend the town's seal to anyone's grudge. {heroName} will not forget it.

ignored.text: {heroName} takes the silence as an answer.

stages.text: {hero} cannot put down the weapon they brought home from the hoard. It is {curse}: {curseText} They ask the town for help, though half of them does not want it.

success.text: The priests chant over the blade for a night and a day. At dawn it is only a fine weapon, and {heroName} sleeps for the first time in weeks.

failure.text: The blade drinks the holy water and hums. Whatever is in it is stronger than the temple's prayers, for now.

success.text: The smiths break the blade, and something screams as it goes. {heroName} is free, and poorer for it.
{heroName} keeps the blade. It is theirs now, curse and all, and it seems pleased.

ignored.text: {heroName} keeps the blade, or the blade keeps them.

decrees.name: Market tolls lifted
decrees.text: No tolls at the market. Stallholders come from further off, settlers follow them, and the treasury feels it.

decrees.name: A pension for the watch's widows
decrees.text: The town keeps the families of the watch it lost. Folk sleep easier for it.

decrees.name: The tavern curfew
decrees.text: The taps close at the evening bell. The lanes are quieter and the town is crosser.

decrees.name: Mended roads
decrees.text: Drained and gravelled roads: carts reach the building sites, and the road brings more hopefuls.

decrees.name: The eased tithe
decrees.text: The farms keep more of the harvest this season, and work the harder for it.

decrees.name: The guild's monopoly
decrees.text: One guild sets the prices in the ward. The treasury takes its share; nobody else likes it.

decrees.name: The levy
decrees.text: Every able hand drills on the green at dawn. The building sites stand half empty.

decrees.name: Merchants keep away
decrees.text: Word went round the trading houses that this town seizes grain. Caravans take the long road.

decrees.name: A quarter for the newcomers
decrees.text: The refugees have a quarter and a voice of their own, and their cousins are coming up the road.

decrees.name: Winter rationing
decrees.text: Every household draws a measured share from the common stores until the thaw.

decrees.name: Wards on the council chamber
decrees.text: Sigils on the lintels and bells that ring for no wind. A charm laid on a councillor is caught at the door.

precedents.text: The gates were opened to the refugees, and the town took them in.
The gates stayed shut while refugees begged outside them.
The mayor sold a guild the trade of a ward.
A hedge-witch was given to the crowd.
The mayor stood between a hedge-witch and the crowd.
The mayor seized a merchant's hoard in the hungry winter.
The mayor made a paladin break their oath of mercy.
The town took a dark patron's gold.
The mayor's heroes talked raiders out of their hold instead of killing them.
Townsfolk carried off in a raid were never brought home.
Heroes brought home townsfolk carried off in a raid.
The mayor sent a hero packing.
The mayor forbade the town's heroes to take gifts from the dark powers.
The mayor let a stranger in a green coat sweeten the wells.
The mayor signed a smiling notary's contract without reading the small print.
The mayor took a crone's apples to cure the fever.
The town found households in its rolls that nobody remembers.
Heroes found the way down to what makes the town forget.
The town dealt with what made it forget its own.
The mayor chose a side between farmers and the goblin families in their hollow.
The town sheltered goblin families the farmers wanted dead.
The town drove starving goblin families out into the hills.
The children of the lanes play at being the town's heroes.

callings.name: Warder of the chamber
callings.text: Keeps wards on the council chamber. A charm laid on a councillor is caught at the door.

callings.name: Truth-seer to the council
callings.text: Sits by the council door and hears every lie as a sour note. A foe's servant on the council is found out far sooner.

callings.name: The town's bard
callings.text: Plays the tavern every night. Spirits rise, and the road hears of it.

callings.name: Oath of the Shield
callings.text: Sworn to the walls. Stronger at the gate, steadier in the lanes.

callings.name: Oath of Mercy
callings.text: Sworn to the weak. The poor lanes are kinder, and the gods notice.

callings.name: Oath of Vengeance
callings.text: Sworn to hunt what preys on the town. Dread ebbs; the town is a grimmer place.

callings.name: Go-between to the Quiet Hand
callings.text: Sits at the thieves' table. Their knives stay off the town, and an envelope comes every week.

callings.name: Informer in the Quiet Hand
callings.text: Sits at the thieves' table and tells the watch. The guild grows hotter until it is exposed.

callings.name: Drillmaster of the militia
callings.text: Drills the militia at dawn. The walls are better held.

callings.name: Strongarm of the works
callings.text: Hauls beams and stone for the builders, for fun. Building goes faster.

callings.name: Preacher at the temple
callings.text: Preaches every rest day. The town's god is honoured and the lanes are calmer.

callings.name: Healer of the poor
callings.text: Tends the sick in the poorer lanes, with salves the town pays for.

callings.name: Keeper of the grove
callings.text: Keeps the old grove. Fields come up greener; less timber is cut.

callings.name: Woodward
callings.text: Chooses which trees fall. The woods and the fields both do better.

callings.name: Warden of the roads
callings.text: Walks the roads with a horn. Carters and settlers feel safer coming.

callings.name: Teacher of the dawn forms
callings.text: Teaches the forms at dawn. Apprentices are calmer and fight less.

callings.name: Trainer of the watch
callings.text: Trains the watch to fight with open hands. Steadier walls, fewer broken heads.

callings.name: Spark of the forges
callings.text: Lights the smiths' fires with wild magic. More tools, and the odd scorched roof.

callings.name: The patron's tithe
callings.text: Gold from the old well every week. Dread grows, and the gods turn away.

callings.name: The town's sage
callings.text: Runs a school of letters and numbers. Clerks are quicker and builders read plans.

callings.name: Warder of the walls
callings.text: Sets wards in the gatehouse stones. The walls are harder to breach.

callings.name: Keeper of the gate keys
callings.text: Holds the gate keys. Nothing comes in after dark unseen.

callings.name: Lantern of the outer wards
callings.text: Walks the lanes outside the walls at night. The newer wards sleep easier.

callings.name: Keeper of the map room
callings.text: Keeps the great map in the town hall. Settlers find their way here, and the wilds seem smaller.

callings.name: Keeper of the whispering relic
callings.text: Keeps a whispering relic at the temple. Pilgrims and the gods come closer; so does something else.

callings.name: The town's herbalist
callings.text: Brews salves and draughts by the apothecary fire. Fevers break sooner.

callings.name: Blesser of the fields
callings.text: Sings to the seed at dusk. The harvest comes up strong.
